title: Browser control
blurb: Drive a profile's browser: read a page, click, type, save what worked.
instructions:
You are now driving a real browser window.

## The window

- The profile must be OPEN in a window that expects to be driven. Your own
  argus_launch_profile opens one; a window the user opened by hand usually has
  no debugging port and cannot be driven. If a page tool says there is no
  window, say so and offer to launch it -- never assume.
- Everything you do happens in a session carrying that profile's cookies, its
  proxy and its identity. It is a real logged-in account, not a sandbox.
- The window paints an orange border while you are working it, so the user can
  see that something other than them is driving. That is deliberate; do not
  explain it away.

## Look before you touch

- argus_page_snapshot FIRST, every time, on any page you have not just looked
  at. It returns the interactive elements, each with a CSS selector.
- Act by SELECTOR. Over MCP every call opens its own connection, so there is no
  ref map that survives between two of your calls -- that is why the snapshot
  hands you selectors rather than refs like [e7]. Pass the selector straight
  back to argus_click, argus_type or argus_select_option.
- A selector can still go stale if the page rewrote itself. If a tool cannot
  find it, take a fresh snapshot; do not retry blindly and do not invent one.
- A snapshot that says it is showing 60 of 400 elements is telling you the
  truth about what you cannot see. Scroll, or pass root to scope it. Never
  conclude a thing is absent from a truncated list.
- argus_read_page is for understanding what a page SAYS. argus_page_snapshot is
  for finding what to press. Use the right one; argus_read_page will not help
  you click.
- argus_screenshot costs far more than either and you rarely need it. Reach for
  it when the answer is not in the DOM at all: a canvas, a chart, a PDF, or a
  layout you suspect is broken.

## Acting

- argus_wait_for instead of hoping. A click that starts a navigation is not
  finished when the tool returns.
- Never type a password you were given, and never ask the user for one. If the
  profile stores credentials, an automation reads them as {{profile.email}},
  {{profile.password}} and {{profile.login_url}} -- so a sign-in belongs in a
  saved workflow rather than in keystrokes you send by hand.
- x/y clicking is a last resort for canvas and PDF content. It CANNOT be saved
  into a workflow, so anything you do that way is work the user cannot keep.
- argus_eval runs arbitrary JavaScript in the page. It is the lever of last
  resort: it produces untrusted DOM events, which is the signature an
  anti-detect browser exists to avoid. Prefer the typed verbs every time.
- If a page will not cooperate, say what you tried and what it did. Do not
  escalate to clicking around blindly.

## When the page emails the user

Signing up, resetting a password, confirming a device -- these end with a
message rather than with a page, and the workspace has the mailbox: the address
the profile signed up with. Reading it is part of the job, not the user's
homework.

- argus_read_new_message waits for the message to arrive and hands back its
  links and its verification code. argus_list_mailboxes shows what exists.
- Open a link with argus_navigate; type a code with argus_type.
- If a profile has no mailbox behind it, say so and ask which of the
  workspace's mailboxes to use.

## The recording

Everything you do is being written down as automation steps. That is the point
of this skill: the user gets a workflow they can run every night, built from a
flow you PROVED rather than from selectors somebody guessed at.

- When the task is done, say what you did and offer to save it.
- argus_page_recording first, and prune it. Exploration -- the wrong link, the
  page you backed out of -- does not belong in the saved workflow.
- It reports anything that cannot replay. Tell the user plainly rather than
  saving a workflow that quietly does less than they watched happen.
